newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Helsinki summit to crown Yeltsin's return.
newsitem.headline: Helsinki summit to crown Yeltsin's return.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin will crown his return to the world stage and the latest of many political comebacks when he flies to Helsinki next week for a summit with U.S. President Bill Clinton.

Yeltsin's health was so fragile that initial plans to hold the summit in the United States were scrapped to bring it closer to Russia. It had seemed in doubt altogether when pneumonia set back Yeltsin's recovery from heart surgery.

But the 66-year-old president, confirming his reputation as a fighter, has stunned political opponents who had written him off by returning to the Kremlin and reasserting his authority with unexpected vigour and the determination of old.

He announced his return by making a government reshuffle, warning opponents that he will get tough if they try to block his reforms and setting out plans in a keynote speech for a better and brighter Russia by the year 2000.

"They should know I am a fighter and I remain a fighter. They shouldn't attack me too hard because I can hit back," Yeltsin warned his political foes in a rare walkabout outside the Kremlin on February 23.

"I want to pass on to my successor a country with a dynamically growing economy, an effective and fair social protection system, a country whose people look to the future with confidence," he told parliament on March 6.
That 25-minute state-of-the-nation speech was seen by Russian politicians as one of two major tests of his health and ability to rule. The other has been identified as the summit on March 19 and 20.

Although he is much thinner than during his energetic re-election campaign in the first half of last year, and still not at his best, Yeltsin's improvement in recent weeks suggests his four-year second presidential term is finally under way.
Yeltsin's health problems are not surprising after a roller-coaster career in which he has fought many battles, taken repeated risks and handled problems on a huge scale.

He rose as a Communist Party official in the Soviet Union, but then became leader of the first legal opposition in the communist superpower, crushed the party and played a pivotal role in destroying the Soviet Union.

Elected Russia's president in 1991, he launched market reforms and helped keep relations with the United States and other Western countries on a good track, particularly at the time of the Soviet Union's collapse in December 1991.
Ties have since cooled, and were not helped by the nearly-two-year conflict in the breakaway Chechnya region which began in 1994. But Yeltsin and Clinton still enjoy a good personal rapport.
Yeltsin's poticial problems after the Chechnya conflict erupted were compounded by two mild heart attacks in 1995 which put him out of action for months.
His popularity was little above zero by the start of 1996 but he pulled out all the stops to fight off communist challenger Gennady Zyuganov to secure re-election on July 3.
He criss-crossed the vast country, keeping to a punishing schedule and adding flourishes such as playing on a swing and dancing the twist at a pop concert.
Gone was the halting walk, the slurred speech and the puffy face which had stirred rumours that heavy drinking was taking its toll.
But the image of the Yeltsin who climbed on a tank in August 1991 to defy a communist-led putsch in Moscow disappeared abruptly when his goal was in sight.

Yeltsin disappeared from the public eye. One doctor said Yeltsin may have had a third heart attack and the president finally announced last September 5 that he had decided to have an operation to be able to return to active life.
He returned to the Kremlin on December 23 but pneumonia forced him to go back to hospital from January 8 to 20.
His walkabout on February 23 signalled his return to the political stage, marked by a government reshuffle intended to give new life to economic reforms.
Yeltsin hit the peak of his power, strength and popularity in August 1991 when he defied a hardline coup against Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev.

A construction engineer by profession, he bucked authority and defeated the odds from early on as a communist official in the Urals industrial city of Sverdlovsk, now Yekaterinburg, and rose to be Moscow party chief in 1985.
He quickly became a candidate member of the ruling Politburo but his demands for faster reform lost him favour and he was disgraced by Gorbachev in 1987.

But in March 1989 he was elected to parliament in the country's first multi-candidate elections. In July 1990, he gambled again and stalked out of the Communist Party, a move which only increased his popularity.
His moral authority slipped in 1993 when he used tanks to crush a bloody rebellion by parliamentary hardliners in Moscow.
In December 1994 he committed what he later acknowledged to be a blunder, sending troops to Chechnya to try to end its drive for independence. Tens of thousands of people were killed.
The threat of a communist return to power kicked him out of his lethargy, prompting a sudden burst of activity for the 1996 election campaign.
His latest reappearance finds him facing a diminished threat form the commuinsts but intent on going down in history as a great reformer.
Boris Nikolayevich Yeltsin was born in a peasant family on February 1, 1931. He has a wife, Naina, two daughters and four grandchildren.
